metadata.title: Teacher collaboration, school innovativeness and innovative teaching in Taiwan: Evidence from TALIS

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for lower secondary teachers in Taiwan, with the TALIS sampling described as stratified random sampling with a target response rate above 75% for schools and teachers. The manuscript reports an overall response rate (56.25%) and provides descriptive statistics for the analytic sample, but it does not report whether TALIS sampling weights or replicate weights were applied in the mediation/measurement modeling. Because the analysis is conducted with AMOS/SEM (confirmatory factor analysis and bootstrapped mediation) rather than ML prediction, the paper does not specify any weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT) or replicate-weight procedure. Therefore, weighting strategy cannot be confirmed from the text; analysts should verify in the original TALIS data documentation whether weights were used when reproducing the results.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are latent constructs measured via Likert-type survey items (teacher collaboration, school innovativeness, innovative teaching) estimated through confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling, not cognitive achievement scores with TALIS/PISA-style plausible values. As a result, plausible values are not applicable to this study’s measurement and mediation framework. Missing data are handled using the expectation-maximization (EM) technique to estimate missing values, which is an imputation approach rather than listwise deletion.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TALIS 2018 data restricted to lower secondary school teachers in Taiwan (one of the 48 TALIS countries/economies). The analytic sample comprises 3835 valid responses; the paper does not further specify additional exclusions beyond the CFA item exclusions (TT3G33H and TT3G33G excluded due to lower factor loadings) and the use of EM to estimate missing values.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Structural equation model fit: RMSEA=0.04, TLI=0.97, GFI=0.98, CFI=0.98, SRMR=0.03, NFI=0.97, AGFI=0.97. Direct effects: Professional collaboration → Innovative teaching β=0.44 (p<0.001); School innovativeness → Innovative teaching β=0.05 (p<0.05). Bootstrapped mediation (95% percentile CI): PC→IT indirect via SI point estimate=0.009, CI [0.001, 0.019], p=0.029; PC→IT total effect=0.399 (CI [0.351, 0.445], p<0.001); ECT→IT direct effect not significant (β=-0.061, CI [-0.133, 0.011]); ECT→SI→IT indirect effect point estimate=0.008, CI [0.017, 0.028], p=0.001; Total effects for ECT→IT=0.399 (reported under total effects in Table 4).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 Lower secondary teachers (Taiwan) the study leveraged Professional collaboration (items), Exchange and coordination (items), and School innovativeness (items) to model Innovative teaching (latent construct), finding that Professional collaboration had a strong direct positive association with innovative teaching (β=0.44, p<0.001) while Exchange and coordination showed no significant direct effect and operated through full mediation via school innovativeness. This indicates that strengthening deeper, interdependent professional collaboration may be more effective for promoting innovative teaching than encouraging surface-level exchanges, with school innovativeness acting as a key mechanism.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for lower secondary teachers in Taiwan (N=3835 valid responses) to examine how two forms of teacher collaboration relate to innovative teaching, with school innovativeness as a mediator. Using confirmatory factor analysis and a structural equation model (AMOS) with EM-based missing value estimation and 5000-sample bootstrapping for mediation, the model fit was good (RMSEA=0.04; CFI=0.98; SRMR=0.03). Professional collaboration showed a significant direct positive effect on innovative teaching (β=0.44, p<0.001), whereas exchange and coordination for teaching did not show a significant direct association and instead influenced innovative teaching through school innovativeness (full mediation). School innovativeness had a small but significant positive effect on innovative teaching (β=0.05, p<0.05). Limitations include reliance on self-reported Likert measures and the absence of explicit reporting on TALIS sampling weights and replicate-weight procedures.
